chain.g: make heir

ety.text: From Middle English enheriten, from Old French enheriter, from Late Latin inhereditare (“make heir”). Displaced native Old English ierfan.

senses.d: To receive (property, a title, etc.), by legal succession or bequest, usually after the previous owner's death.
ex: After Grandad died, I inherited the house.
When we took office, we inherited a total catastrophe.
Lucky old Daniel – his grandfather died rich, and he's inherited.

senses.d: To take possession of as a right (especially in Biblical translations).
ex: Your descendants will inherit the earth.

senses.d: To receive a characteristic from one's ancestors by genetic transmission.
ex: Let's hope the baby inherits his mother's looks and his father's intelligence.

senses.d: To derive from people or conditions previously in force.
ex: This country has inherited an invidious class culture.

senses.d: To derive (existing functionality) from a superclass.
ex: ModalWindow inherits all the properties and methods of Window.

senses.d: To derive a new class from (a superclass).
ex: For example, the following two code segments, from different assemblies, show how easy it is to inherit a class from another assembly.
This, or else nothing, will inherit her

ety.text: Inherited from Middle English enheritaunce, inheritaunce, borrowed from Anglo-Norman, Old French enheritaunce, from enheriter. By surface analysis, inherit + -ance.

senses.d: The passing of title to an estate upon death.
That which a person is entitled to inherit, by law or testament, such as the part of an estate (i.e., a portion).
The act or mechanism of inheriting; the state of having inherited.
ex: The Indo-European languages share various similarities as a result of their inheritance from a common ancestor.

senses.d: The biological attributes passed hereditarily from ancestors to their offspring.
The mechanism whereby parts of a superclass are available to instances of its subclass.
